papers.title: A five-day Mindfulness Based Intervention to reduce burnout and psychological distress in UK Medical Students
papers.abstract: Background Medical professionals face significant work overload, with excessive job demands often strongly associated with attrition and burnout. Consequences of burnout include reduced job satisfaction, absenteeism, reduced patient care, lower patient satisfaction and increased healthcare costs. UK Medical students are also at high risk of burnout. Mindfulness-based interventions are effective individual-level treatments, however more research is required to investigate the efficacy of mindfulness for healthcare professionals and students. Method Four cohorts of second-year medical students at Cardiff University participated in a five-day, in-person mindfulness-based intervention. Pre (T1) and post (T2) intervention and follow-up (T3) survey data were collected online using validated outcome measures for burnout, psychological distress and wellbeing. Results Statistical analysis of data from 69 participants found a statistically significant improvement post intervention (T2) for current energy, calmness, focus and stress (all P=0.001). Statistically significant improvements in psychological distress (Core-10, P=0.001), Burnout (OLBI, P=0.023), and Wellbeing (WHO5, P=0.37) with small, large and small effect sizes respectively; maintained at follow-up (T3). Satisfaction ratings were consistently high, and completion rate was 100%. Discussion Medical schools should consider implementing mindfulness-based interventions into medical curricula, as a feasible and acceptable student selected preventative tool to address burnout and incorporate student perspectives on delivery; to prevent mental ill health in medical professionals.

papers.title: Career development awards are associated with lower career-long research attrition risk in Veterans Affairs investigators.
papers.abstract: Objective:To investigate research attrition and the associated factors among US Department of Veterans Affairs investigators with and without a prior Career Development Award (CDA) from fiscal year 2008 to 2026. Design: Retrospective cohort study. Methods: Investigators whose CDA ended between October 2008 and March 2026 were identified from the Research Analysis and Forecasting Tool (RAFT) database and compared to non-CDA peers. Extracted descriptive variables included sex, investigator type, doctoral degree, salary source, specialty, and research area. Attrition, derived from the electronic Project Management and Information System, was defined when an investigator ceased serving as a principal or coinvestigator on VA-funded research. Analysis utilized attrition percentages, crude count ratios (CR), chi-squared statistics, and multivariable binomial regression to assess adjusted odds ratios (ORadj). Results: Investigators with a prior CDA were 42% less likely to attrite from VA research engagement compared to non-CDA counterparts (CR 95% CI, 0.50-0.67, p<.001). They maintained high engagement regardless of demographic or professional variables (engagement ranges: 66.7%-93.8%). Clinician-scientists were 34% less likely to attrite from science (ORadj 0.54) compared to non-clinician scientists. The 1.68-times higher crude attrition risk for non-VA salaried investigators became non-significant after adjusting for other factors. Attrition was significantly higher in basic science and engineering (ORadj 3.90), endocrinology, metabolism, and nutrition (ORadj 4.24), infectious disease (ORadj 3.80), aging and geriatrics (ORadj 3.56), and cardiopulmonary and vascular research (ORadj 2.70) compared to health services and epidemiology. Conclusion: Prior CDA recipients demonstrate significantly lower research attrition in VA research.

papers.title: Survey of Physician Attitudes on Artificial Intelligence
papers.abstract: ObjectiveTo better understand how physicians view the potential use of artificial intelligence (AI) in their practices. MethodWe conducted an online cross-sectional survey of 1,258 physicians (MD, DO, MBBS or equivalent) in the United States (US) and Canada from December 2023 through February 2026. The survey contained 34 questions focused on 6 areas: (1) demographics, (2) training, (3) clinical benefits, (4) clinical concerns, (5) clinical AI prediction tools, and (6) generative AI. ResultsA total of 130 completed surveys were received (response rate, 10%). Top specialties included psychiatry (46.2%), internal medicine (14.6%) and pediatrics (13.8%). A total of 16.9% had training in computer science or information technology and 40.8% in statistics. Nearly half (46.9%) had no formal training in AI and were self-taught. Those with training in AI received it through vendors or at work. Sixty to seventy percent thought AI would provide diagnostic aid or treatment recommendations, but half did not feel adequately trained to safely use AI in practice. Over 70% thought it could help with administrative tasks. More than 80% were worried about errors, misinformation, or biases in the data. ConclusionThere is a growing sense that AI in medicine could be helpful with specific tasks. Ongoing training, education, and study are needed to determine how AI will best integrate into clinical practice. Artificial intelligence (AI) is rapidly being marketed for and integrated into clinical medicine. Previous physician surveys have shown that physicians are optimistic, yet cautious, about its implementation. This study utilizes a novel survey tool to assess physician attitudes toward the integration of AI in practice, highlighting the desire for ongoing education around and monitoring of AI among physicians in the United States and Canada. There is a growing recognition that AI, while a powerful tool, may harbor biases, promulgate misinformation, and lead to harm to patients, and requires ongoing training and oversight by humans.

papers.title: Who Publishes During Residency? A Systematic Review and Meta-Analysis of Peer-Reviewed Publication Among Residents in the United States
papers.abstract: Background/ObjectivesThe Accreditation Council for Graduate Medical Education requires US residents to participate in scholarship, but no review has pooled how many physician residents publish during training. We estimated the proportion who published at least 1 peer-reviewed article during residency and compared specialties. MethodsIn October 2026, we searched PubMed, Europe PMC, OpenAlex, ERIC, and ClinicalTrials.gov (protocol, osf.io/eupxr). AI agents screened records, two AI models from different developers independently extracted outcome data, and an author decided every disagreement against the source. Proportions were pooled with random-effects generalized linear mixed models. ResultsOf 172 included studies, 32 US studies (13,450 residents) reported the primary outcome. The pooled proportion was 59.6% (95% CI, 48.7%-69.6%). Surgical specialties had 68.7% and medical specialties 29.6%. Adjusted for data source and pre-intervention status, the odds of publishing in medical cohorts were less than one-third of those in surgical cohorts: odds ratio (OR), 0.28 (95% CI, 0.12-0.63). Conclusions: About 60% of US residents publish during training, but specialties differ widely, and medical specialties have the most room for improvement. Key PointsO_ST_ABSQuestionC_ST_ABSWhat proportion of US residents publish at least 1 peer-reviewed article during residency, and does it differ by specialty? FindingsIn 32 US studies with 13,450 residents, the pooled proportion was 59.6%: 68.7% in surgical and 29.6% in medical specialties. After adjustment for data source and pre-intervention status, the odds of publishing in medical cohorts were less than one-third of those in surgical cohorts (OR, 0.28). MeaningAbout 6 in 10 US residents publish during training, and medical specialties have the most room for improvement.

papers.title: Calibrated large language models demonstrate a consistent advantage in a randomized longitudinal medical education intervention
papers.abstract: Medical trainees increasingly use large language models to review lecture material, but the educational value of that output depends on how it is generated, with prompt and model choice rarely measured. We tested a calibrated pipeline converting Neurology Grand Rounds recordings into summaries and quizzes in a year-long randomized study. In Phase 1, six summary and six question prompts across two models were scored with 2,692 rubric annotations. Claude Prompt 0 produced the best summaries (composite 76.9%) and GPT Prompt 1 the best questions (79.6%); quality varied widely by prompt, and neither model won both tasks. In Phase 2, students in 11 clerkship cohorts over a year were randomized within cohort to receive a summary before each quiz. Summary recipients reported reviewing more and studying faster and scored higher in 9 of 11 cohorts (p = 0.026), although the between-student difference was small (+0.28 of 10 points; P = 0.28).

papers.title: Medical students and clinical teachers experiences and perceptions of using AI-based simulated patients in psychiatry clinical skills training, a qualitative analysis
papers.abstract: BackgroundSimulation-based teaching is central to undergraduate psychiatry education, supporting the development of key clinical skills. Recent advances in generative artificial intelligence (AI), and digital avatars, have enabled the development of AI-driven simulated patients (ASP) that may offer flexible, repeatable learning opportunities. However, there is limited evidence regarding the perceptions of medical students regarding the use of such tools in psychiatry education. AimsTo explore medical students attitudes and beliefs towards the use of AI simulated patients for psychiatry clinical skills training, to inform future educational development and integration. MethodMedical students were invited to participate through university mailing lists and departmental and student networks. Interested participants self-enrolled by responding to the invitation. Clinical teachers were recruited through the Royal College of Psychiatrists South East Division newsletter. All participants gave both written and verbal consent. A total of sixteen medical students participated across two focus groups. Nine clinical teachers participated across three groups. Each session included a 10-minute hands-on interaction with an exemplar AI based simulation tool, which was developed by the research team. The tool was built in May 2025 using OpenAIs ChatGPT voice feature (Advanced Voice Mode, powered by GPT-4o), Streamlit (v1.45), and LangChain (v0.3.x). Each AI simulated patients interaction was followed by a facilitated group discussion. Sessions were audio-recorded and transcribed verbatim for subsequent thematic analysis. ResultsParticipants identified both potential benefits and limitations of AI simulated patients in psychiatry education. It was seen as useful for early communication skills training, by offering flexible, low-pressure practice. However, concerns were raised about how well the avatars functioned technically and how accurately they could present people experiencing mental illness, as well as their limited realism compared with actor-based teaching and real patient encounters. Key priorities for future development included improving emotional realism, expanding scenario options, and ensuring closer alignment with communication skills teaching and institutional systems to support meaningful curriculum integration. ConclusionsParticipants recognised the potential of AI simulated patients for undergraduate psychiatry education but identified key barriers to engagement, particularly system reliability and trust, realism representation and institutional access. Addressing these considerations will be important for effective integration, supported by ongoing student involvement.

papers.title: Interpreting Self-Reported Outcomes After AI-Assisted Writing Workshops: An Aggregate Sensitivity Analysis of Educational Claims
papers.abstract: Artificial intelligence writing workshops are increasingly used in health-professions education, but immediate self-reports can be interpreted as evidence of learning or ethical competence beyond what they measure. This study applied an aggregate-data interpretation framework to a published single-institution evaluation of a hands-on AI-assisted academic-writing workshop. Public counts and item summaries were classified by construct, summarized with binomial working-model intervals for observed respondents, and reanalyzed with complete registered-list identification intervals that assigned every questionnaire nonrespondent first to the non-positive and then to the positive category. Among 64 respondents, 54 reported improved understanding, or 84.4 percent, with a working-model interval of 73.6 percent to 91.3 percent. Confidence and perceived ethical improvement were each reported by 45 respondents, or 70.3 percent, with intervals of 58.2 percent to 80.1 percent. Across 80 registrants, unrestricted nonresponse yielded identification intervals of 67.5 percent to 87.5 percent for perceived improvement and 56.2 percent to 76.2 percent for both confidence and ethical improvement. Positive delivery ratings were common. However, these measures did not assess objective knowledge, writing quality, source verification, ethical decision-making, or sustained practice. The evidence supports bounded descriptions of respondent experience only; effectiveness claims require linked objective assessment and delayed follow-up.

papers.title: Doctors Experiences of Interruptions in the Digital Age and the Impact on Clinical Care in England
papers.abstract: ObjectiveInterruptions are frequent in clinical care globally and associated with inefficiency, cognitive burden, and patient safety risks. Existing research into interruptions reflects paper-based workflows, and "digital distraction" studies often focus on personal device use. There is little research regarding interruptions produced by mandated digital infrastructures such as Electronic Health Records (EHRs) and clinical messaging platforms. This study aims to examine how mandated digital systems shape the form, experience, and meaning of interruptions in English outpatient care, and how doctors attempt to manage these demands. Methods and AnalysisWe conducted a qualitative analysis of focus group and interview data from a larger study of interruptions in outpatient care. Participants were 42 UK outpatient care doctors across specialties and experience levels, recruited via a screener survey and stratified into six groups based on experience level and self-reported patient complexity (trainee, 0-19 years, and 20+ years experience, each divided into high and low complexity). Data were analysed using Reflexive Thematic Analysis, with interpretation informed by the combined lens of Cognitive Load Theory and Social Identity theory; a pairing not previously applied together to interruptions, capturing both the cognitive and social-relational dimensions of digital interruptions. Analysis as structured deductively around these theories while remaining open to inductive, novel insights. ResultsFour themes captured digitally mediated interruption. Mandated systems normalised constant availability, making interruption a persistent condition of work. Digital tools acted as cognitive amplifiers, increasing extraneous cognitive load through fragmented interfaces, multi-window navigation, and technical unreliability, with perceived safety risks around patient-context switching. Digital coordination occurred without social cues, weakening visibility and contextual signals that support judgements of relevance, urgency, and responsibility, contributing to interpersonal friction. Doctors sought to reclaim control through individual strategies, including limiting exposure to channels and selectively embracing digital prompts where they supported safety or care quality. ConclusionMandated digital infrastructures transform interruption into continuous, cognitively disruptive, and socially ambiguous demands. Mitigation requires system- and organisation-level solutions beyond individual workarounds. Key MessagesO_ST_ABSWhat is already known on this topicC_ST_ABSInterruptions are a known source of cognitive burden and safety risk in clinical care, but research has focused on paper-based workflows and personal device distraction, leaving interruptions from mandated systems like EHRs poorly understood. What this study addsThis study shows mandated digital systems turn interruption into a constant background condition of work, increasing cognitive load through fragmented interfaces and weakening the social cues doctors rely on to judge urgency and responsibility. How this study might affect research, practice or policyAs healthcare becomes increasingly digitally mediated, existing boundaries around availability, communication etiquette, and patient safety need to be revisited as an organisational priority, rather than a challenge for individual doctors to manage alone. This includes clearer digital communication norms and boundaries, safer alert and task-resumption design to reduce patient-context switching risk, and policies that formally protect time for cognitively demanding digital work.

papers.title: Widespread Programs, Limited Evidence: How U.S. MD-Granting Medical Schools Define, Measure, and Evaluate Student Well-Being Efforts
papers.abstract: PurposeTo characterize how U.S. MD-granting medical schools define wellness aims, assess student well-being, evaluate program effectiveness, and analyze and report outcomes. MethodFrom June 2025 through September 2026, the authors surveyed all 159 Liaison Committee on Medical Education-accredited U.S. MD-granting schools using a web-based instrument. Analyses used item-specific denominators for partial responses. Among 84 schools answering five linked items, the authors examined completion of the sequence from defined aims to reported outcomes. Exploratory analyses examined associations between explicit wellness competencies and the remaining practices. ResultsOf 159 schools, 107 (67.3%) provided substantive responses. Of the 84 schools that answered all five linked items, 2 (2.4%) reported the complete sequence, and 22 (26.2%) reported none. Explicit wellness competencies were reported by 23/91 schools (25.3%); 38/91 (41.8%) were unsure whether any existed. Schools reported formal assessment of student well-being (48/91, 52.7%) and formal program evaluation (43/90, 47.8%). Among schools that evaluated, 39/42 (92.9%) used Association of American Medical Colleges national surveys, whereas 14/42 (33.3%) used any standardized longitudinal or pre/post measure. Schools rarely analyzed outcomes by student demographic characteristics (16/89, 18.0%), and none reported publishing outcomes in full. Schools with explicit wellness competencies reported more of the remaining practices (median 2 vs 1, P = .007), with associations concentrated in program evaluation and outcome reporting. Wellness infrastructure was common: dedicated curricula (65/107, 60.7%), learning communities (85/98, 86.7%), mistreatment reporting or prevention policies in clinical training (89/97, 91.8%), and wellness committees (73/84, 86.9%). ConclusionsResponding U.S. medical schools commonly reported wellness infrastructure, but few reported a complete sequence from defined wellness aims to reported outcomes. Gaps in explicit wellness competencies, assessment, program evaluation, and outcome reporting limit schools ability to judge program effectiveness. Explicit wellness competencies were associated with more evaluation and reporting practices; whether they improve program effectiveness remains unclear.

papers.title: Neonatal Resuscitation Training in Australian Public Birthing and Newborn Care Facilities: A National Cross-Sectional Survey
papers.abstract: BackgroundThe stabilisation of infants at birth is vital for survival and relies on clinicians being appropriately trained in neonatal resuscitation. The effectiveness of resuscitation is influenced by the skills, knowledge and equipment available to the responding clinician. In Australia, the absence of a standardised neonatal resuscitation training programme may contribute to variations in training practices. This study aimed to describe current training practices across Australian public services and explore educators perceptions of opportunities for national standardisation. MethodsA cross-sectional survey was distributed to educators and representatives from birth and newborn care public facilities across Australia. A questionnaire was developed to gain knowledge on how newborn resuscitation is taught detailing staffing, equipment and training requirements. Results197 completed responses were received. Responses were received from all Australian states and territories and levels of maternity/neonatal services. Accreditation in neonatal resuscitation was required by 173 (87.8%) of respondents programmes with training occurring at annual (n=95, 47.7%) or more frequent (n=21, 10.7%) intervals. NeoResus (n=134, 67.5%), Neonatal Advanced Life Support (n=45, 22.8%) and Newborn Life Support Training (n=41, 21.3%) were the most popular training programmes. Substantial variation was identified in equipment used for training. Most respondents (n=174, 88.3%) reported a need for a standardised national training programme. ConclusionsNeonatal resuscitation training is widely available in Australian public facilities, but reported requirements, programmes, content, assessment methods and training resources vary. These findings support the development of standardised neonatal resuscitation training to promote consistent preparedness across Australian healthcare settings. O_LIWhat is already known on this topic Regular neonatal resuscitation training is recommended by international guidelines and is associated with improved neonatal outcomes. Previous Australian studies have identified a variation in training access and requirements, but contemporary national data are lacking. C_LIO_LIWhat this study adds - summarise what we now know as a result of this study that we did not know before This study provides the first national baseline of neonatal resuscitation training practices across Australian healthcare services. It identifies substantial differences in training requirements, programme delivery and educational resources, providing support and information to inform a standardised national approach. C_LIO_LIHow this study might affect research, practice or policy - summarise the implications of this study The findings provide evidence to support development of coordinated national approach to neonatal resuscitation training and may inform future standards, educational policy and research to improve education. C_LI

papers.title: Development and Feasibility of a Communication Accommodation Training Module for Health Profession Students
papers.abstract: ObjectivesHealth professions students often receive limited training on how to adjust their communication for patients whose first language is not English (LX), despite the risks for diagnosis, treatment, and patient trust. Based on Communication Accommodation Theory, we developed a brief module to improve students awareness and knowledge of strategic communication adjustments for LX patients. MethodsWe tested feasibility in a single-group, pre-post pilot study guided by the Kirkpatrick framework with undergraduate (n=22) and graduate (n=41) speech-language pathology and psychology students in Massachusetts and North Carolina. The module included instructional content, video and audio examples, interactive activities, and a podcast. Learning was assessed with knowledge checks, and self-reported facilitative and resistant accommodation with the Communication Accommodation Behavior Scale (CABS). After training, students rated their confidence and likelihood of using accommodation strategies. ResultsAt both sites, facilitative accommodation increased and resistant accommodation decreased significantly, with a larger decrease at the undergraduate site. Knowledge-check accuracy was high at both time points, suggesting a ceiling effect. Students reported moderate-to-high confidence in adapting their speech and high likelihood of using a learned strategy in future clinical encounters. ConclusionsA brief module can be feasibly delivered across institutions and is associated with short-term improvements in self-reported communication accommodation. Practice implicationsWe recommend future work evaluate whether these changes translate into clinical behavior long-term and refine knowledge-check items to better capture learning gains.

papers.title: Assessing Knowledge and Risk Perception of Mosquitoes and Mosquito-Borne Viruses Among Medical Students in Cyprus: A Cross-Sectional MosquitoWise Study
papers.abstract: BackgroundCyprus has transitioned into a high-alert zone for mosquito-borne viruses. This necessitates a proactive assessment of its future physicians. Following the 2022 re-establishment of Aedes aegypti in Larnaca and Aedes albopictus in Limassol, Cyprus, the island is now biologically primed for local outbreaks of dengue, Zika and chikungunya, alongside Culex-borne West Nile virus. This study assessed medical students knowledge and risk perception. MethodsA cross-sectional online survey administered the validated MosquitoWise Health Belief Model instrument to undergraduate-entry and graduate-entry students at a university in Cyprus in mid-2026. ResultsOf 1023 students, 119 responded (11.6%), with pre-clinical students overrepresented (p<0.001). Mean knowledge was 5.43/9, stronger on mosquito biology (72.5%) than virus knowledge (54.2%). Median severity was 6.00/7 against susceptibility 4.25/7. Knowledge differed by study stage (p<0.001), correlated with severity (rs = 0.399) but not susceptibility. ConclusionsThis study establishes a critical baseline for pre-clinical medical students in Cyprus. Overall, participants performed better on mosquito biology when compared to mosquito-borne viruses and how they spread. Our findings highlight the value of integrating theoretical microbiology with clinical practice in medical education to enhance physicians preparedness for the changing landscape of newly emerging infections in Cyprus and across Europe as a whole.

papers.title: KNOWLEDGE OF METABOLIC SYNDROME, LIFESTYLE RISK BEHAVIOURS AND PREVENTIVE PRACTICES AMONG WOMEN ATTENDING KASOA POLYCLINIC, GHANA: A CROSS-SECTIONAL STUDY.
papers.abstract: BackgroundMetabolic syndrome is a cluster of cardiometabolic risk factors that may increase the risk of cardiovascular disease and type 2 diabetes, and African studies report a higher prevalence in women than in men. Prevention may depend, in part, on whether women recognise the condition and its modifiable risk factors. Relatively little appears to be known about this among women using primary-level health facilities in fast-growing peri-urban areas of Ghana. ObjectiveTo assess knowledge of metabolic syndrome, describe lifestyle risk behaviours, self-reported cardiometabolic conditions and preventive practices, and examine selected lifestyle correlates of self-reported diabetes and hypertension among women attending Kasoa Polyclinic, Ghana. MethodsA descriptive cross-sectional survey was conducted in June and July 2024 among 174 women aged 18-45 years recruited by convenience sampling. A structured, interviewer-assisted questionnaire covered knowledge, lifestyle behaviours, self-reported diagnoses and preventive practices. Data were summarised as frequencies and percentages, and associations were examined with Pearsons chi-square test. ResultsOnly 37 women (21.3%) described metabolic syndrome as a condition that raises the risk of heart disease and type 2 diabetes, 40 (23.0%) identified central (apple-shaped) fat as the high-risk pattern and 31 (17.8%) knew that dietary recommendations exist. Most reported no weekly physical activity (116; 66.7%), daily sugary drinks (109; 62.6%), daily processed or fast food (100; 57.5%), high stress (103; 59.2%), and less than six hours sleep (94; 54.0%). Self-reported diagnoses were hypertension in 60 (34.5%) and type 2 diabetes in 49 (28.2%). Fifty-nine (33.9%) had never received advice on prevention and 105 (60.3%) did not monitor their weight or waist. Self-reported diabetes was associated with short sleep (36.2% among those sleeping under six hours; p = 0.035) and with stress level (p = 0.028), being most frequent among women reporting low stress. Self-reported hypertension was more common with high stress (42.7%; p = 0.022) and with some physical activity (p = 0.005). ConclusionWomen attending this polyclinic appeared to have limited understanding of metabolic syndrome and a high burden of modifiable risk behaviours. Routine counselling on diet, activity, sleep, and weight monitoring at the polyclinic may be warranted. The bivariate, self-reported associations should be interpreted cautiously.

papers.title: How should doctors manage workplace interruptions? A qualitative study in UK hospital outpatient departments
papers.abstract: BackgroundInterruptions are common in hospital outpatient departments (OPDs) and are linked to error. Many are clinically necessary, so the aim is to regulate them. Most interventions target the individual clinician. Little is known about how doctors manage interruptions in practice or what makes their strategies work. MethodsQualitative study using focus groups and interviews with 42 doctors working in UK National Health Service OPDs (19 sessions, September to November 2025). Participants were purposively sampled by clinical experience and self-reported patient complexity. Data were analysed using Framework Analysis, informed by Cognitive Load Theory and Social Identity Theory. ResultsWe developed four themes. (1) Pre-emptive protection of attention. Doctors withdrew, signalled unavailability and set thresholds for interrupting. These depended on colleagues learning and sharing the norm, which staff rotation eroded. (2) Sharing the burden through team coordination. Designated roles and time-limited rotas moved interruptions to colleagues with capacity set aside for them and made interrupting legitimate. (3) Real-time cognitive repair. Doctors asked interrupters to wait while they secured the task, and rebuilt the consultation on return, sometimes with the patients help. Asking a colleague to wait depended on seniority or team membership; some trainees described difficulty doing this with senior colleagues. (4) Organisational recognition as the precondition for sustainable regulation. Where supervision was built into job plans, the interruptions it generated were expected and doctors held capacity in reserve for them. Advice, vetting and telephone queries were rarely counted as work. ConclusionsEach strategy served a cognitive purpose, and social and organisational conditions decided whether it was perceived to work. Interventions could make norms shared and roles explicit, count interruption work in job plans and keep routes open for junior staff to raise concerns. Evaluations should ask who is able to use them. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPICInterruptions are common in clinical work and can disrupt task completion, while most interventions focus on individual clinicians and have shown mixed effects. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDSDoctors described strategies to protect attention, redistribute interruptions and repair disrupted tasks, but their use depended on shared norms, legitimate roles, social standing and organisational capacity. Some trainees described difficulty asking senior colleagues to wait, although trainee representation in this sample was limited. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICYDepartments could agree urgency thresholds alongside clear routes for non-urgent requests, use time-limited roles for queries and recognise advice and supervision in workload planning. Evaluations should assess who can use these arrangements and whether staff can still escalate concerns.

papers.title: BIRTH SPACING AND UNDER-FIVE CHILD SURVIVAL IN GHANA: EVIDENCE FROM THE 2022 DEMOGRAPHIC AND HEALTH SURVEY.
papers.abstract: BackgroundShort birth intervals are a well-documented, modifiable risk factor for child death in low- and middle-income countries, yet nationally representative evidence from Ghanas most recent Demographic and Health Survey has not been fully examined. This study assessed the association between the preceding birth interval and under-five mortality using the 2022 Ghana Demographic and Health Survey. MethodsThe analysis used the complete birth history reported by women aged 15-49 years. The cohort comprised births occurring 60-119 completed months (5-10 years) before the survey, which allowed a complete five-year observation window for under-five survival (n = 8,418; 397 deaths). Spacing models were restricted to second-or-higher-order births with a defined preceding interval (n = 6,340; 282 deaths), categorised as under 18, 18-23, 24-35 (reference), 36-47, and 48 or more months. Crude and adjusted odds ratios were estimated using survey-weighted, Taylor-linearised logistic regression, adjusting for birth order, child sex, plurality, maternal age, residence, region, maternal education, wealth quintile, and marital status. ResultsWeighted under-five mortality in the cohort was 45.4 per 1,000 live births (4.54%). Among second-or-higher-order births, weighted mortality fell from 9.3% after intervals of under 18 months and 8.0% after 18-23 months to 4.2%, 3.2%, and 3.5% after 24-35, 36-47, and 48 or more months, respectively. Relative to 24-35 months, the adjusted odds of death were higher after intervals of under 18 months (adjusted odds ratio [AOR] 2.58, 95% confidence interval [CI] 1.48-4.49, p < 0.001) and 18-23 months (AOR 2.09, 95% CI 1.33-3.29, p = 0.001); longer intervals did not differ from the reference. Multiple birth (AOR 2.48, 95% CI 1.33-4.63) and having a mother who was never in union (AOR 3.25, 95% CI 1.29-8.17) were also associated with higher odds of death, and marked regional variation persisted after adjustment. ConclusionA short preceding birth interval, particularly one of under 18 months, was independently associated with an approximately two-to two-and-a-half-fold increase in the odds of under-five death in this nationally representative sample. The findings support continued investment in postpartum family planning to help women space births at least 24 months apart, alongside closer attention to multiple births, unmarried mothers, and the regions carrying the greatest burden.

papers.title: Who carries the cost of interruptions? A qualitative study of doctors in UK hospital outpatient departments
papers.abstract: BackgroundHospital outpatient departments (OPDs) deliver specialist care at scale, under close scrutiny over waiting times. Interruptions are common in this setting and are linked to error. Little is known about how they cause harm, for whom, and under what conditions. MethodsQualitative study using focus groups and interviews with 42 doctors working in UK National Health Service OPDs (19 sessions, September to November 2025). Participants were purposively sampled by clinical experience and self-reported patient complexity. Data were analysed using the Framework Method, informed by Cognitive Load Theory and Social Identity Theory, with independent double coding of 10% of transcripts and participant validation. ResultsWe developed four themes. (1) Interruptions as a structural and increasingly ambiguous feature of clinical work. Interruptions were a normal part of clinical coordination, but new communication channels lacked shared norms about urgency, so each doctor had to judge what mattered. (2) The hidden cognitive cost of interruptions. The main cost came from returning to the interrupted task. This cost grew with complexity and was only partly offset by experience. (3) The social fabric of interruption burden. Transient teams weakened the norms that regulate interrupting, and approachability and hierarchy concentrated the burden on particular doctors. (4) The social amplification of cognitive burden. Understaffing multiplied cognitive costs. Doctors used familiarity and track record to decide which requests deserved attention, so concerns from junior or unfamiliar colleagues risked being discounted. ConclusionsInterruptions are structural, and their impact depends on cognitive and social conditions. Reducing interruption frequency alone may miss the main risk. Interventions should support task resumption, protect capacity at busy times, rebuild shared communication norms and take account of the receivers capacity when designing escalation. WHAT IS ALREADY KNOWN ON THIS TOPICInterruptions are common in clinical work and are linked to error, and laboratory studies place much of their cost in resuming the interrupted task. WHAT THIS STUDY ADDSIn UK hospital outpatient departments, doctors accounts were consistent with these known mechanisms and suggest two further ones. Unfamiliar teams add cognitive load because each request has to be judged on its content, and under pressure, concerns raised by junior or unfamiliar colleagues may be discounted by the person receiving them. HOW THIS STUDY MIGHT AFFECT RESEARCH, PRACTICE OR POLICYInterventions should support task resumption, set shared norms about urgency, protect doctors capacity at busy times and design escalation with the receivers capacity in mind.

papers.title: Back to work MD - Experiences of internal medicine physicians returning to work after parental leave
papers.abstract: BackgroundParenthood in medicine is an experience fraught with challenges that begin in the pre-conception phase and persist as physician-parents navigate their dual role. MethodsThis study aims to understand the experiences of physician-parents (both childbearing and non-childbearing) returning to work after parental leave. Physicians, including residents, affiliated with the University of Torontos Department of Medicine internal medicine division who had a child within the last ten years were invited to participate in a self-administered electronic survey from June2022 to 30June 2023. Data were summarized using descriptive statistics. ResultsTwenty-nine respondents took part in the survey; 79% were staff physicians while the remaining were trainees at the time of the survey. At the time their first child was born, 48% were staff members and 52% were trainees. The median duration of parental leave was 5 months (range 1-12 months). Among those for whom lactation was applicable, 76% reported that they continued their lactation efforts on returning to work, while 24% chose not to. Thirty five percent (35%, n=6/17) of respondents cited that they were not provided with duty hour modifications when required. Many respondents (46%) felt guilty about burdening their co-workers for requesting accommodations for childcare. When requested to rate their experiences of balancing their personal and professional lives on a scale of 1-10 (1 being "impossible to maintain" and 10 being "extremely easy to maintain"), most respondents (66%) chose a rating of 5 or less. ConclusionThis study supports previous findings that physician-parents face a myriad of challenges integrating their roles in medicine and parenthood. A change in culture is required to support and normalize parenthood for physicians and foster sustainability and productivity in academic medicine.

papers.title: Doctors experiences of interruptions in UK secondary care outpatient clinics: a cross-sectional survey of prevalence, consequences and management strategies
papers.abstract: ObjectivesTo examine the prevalence of interruptions during UK secondary care outpatient consultations, their association with clinician mental workload, and the strategies clinicians use to manage them. DesignNationwide cross-sectional online survey. SettingSecondary care outpatient clinics, United Kingdom. ParticipantsA sample of 465 UK secondary care doctors across a range of grades and specialties, recruited through a medical defence organisations network. Primary and secondary outcome measuresMental workload (NASA Task Load Index, Raw-TLX); interruption frequency; perceived cognitive impact of interruptions; task resumption difficulty; perceived social effects on colleague interactions and team cohesion; and interruption-management strategy use. Results61.1% of clinicians reported being interrupted often or very often, and mean overall workload was high (Raw-TLX 66.2, SD 11.5). Interruption frequency, patient complexity and perceived cognitive impact were each associated with higher workload across multiple NASA-TLX subscales. In fully adjusted models, interruption frequency retained independent associations with overall workload ({beta} = 1.79, p = 0.004) and temporal demand ({beta} = 0.94, p < 0.001). Task resumption difficulty was associated with worse perceived performance ({beta} = -0.59, p = 0.014), while perceiving interruptions as socially positive was associated with better performance ({beta} = 0.75, p = 0.003) and lower frustration ({beta} = -1.16, p < 0.001). Years of experience showed only small effects, and self-reported strategy use (38.7%) was not consistently associated with lower workload. Exploratory natural language processing of open-text descriptions identified three strategy clusters; cognitive offloading, anticipating and preparing, and blunt responses, with distinct emotional profiles. ConclusionsInterruptions were commonly reported during UK secondary care outpatient consultations and were associated with measurable cognitive and temporal burden. The perceived social framing of interruptions was independently associated with frustration and self-rated performance. Binary strategy use showed no consistent workload association, indicating a need for system-level approaches addressing interruption frequency, task resumption support and the social context of interruptions rather than reliance on individual coping. Strengths and limitations of this studyO_LITo our knowledge, this is the first national survey of interruptions in UK secondary care outpatient consultations, spanning a wide range of specialties, grades and career stages (0-52 years post-qualification). C_LIO_LIMental workload was measured using the NASA Task Load Index, a validated multidimensional instrument, allowing workload to be decomposed into cognitive, temporal, physical and affective components. C_LIO_LIOpen-text descriptions of interruption-management strategies were analysed using natural language processing, revealing heterogeneity in strategy type that binary coding alone would have obscured. C_LIO_LIThe cross-sectional design precludes causal inference, and the direction of the association between perceived interruption frequency and workload cannot be established. C_LIO_LIRecruitment through a single medical defence organisations network, together with an indeterminate eligible denominator, means this was a convenience sample in which non-response bias cannot be excluded. C_LI

papers.title: Success Among Ethnic Minorities and International Medical Graduates in UK Medical Speciality Recruitment: A Longitudinal Analysis of NHS England Data (2021-2025)
papers.abstract: BackgroundWhile overall application volume by ethnic minority doctors into UK postgraduate medical training has expanded significantly, workforce diversity varies substantially across specialties. Previous reports have suggested that doctors from certain ethnic backgrounds and international medical graduates (IMGs) experience lower likelihoods of securing training posts, but granular longitudinal evaluations across all specialty training levels and recruitment stages remained limited. Therefore, this study evaluates longitudinal trends in self-reported ethnicity and country of qualification across postgraduate medical training in England between 2021 and 2025, maps specialty representation, and tests the hypothesis that recruitment success rates differ significantly between ethnic minority and White baseline applicants. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective national longitudinal analysis of mandatory NHS specialty recruitment data across England from 2021 to 2025, encompassing over 300,000 applications across ST1/CT1 (entry-level) and ST3+ (higher specialty) pathways. Applicants were categorised into census-aligned broad and granular ethnic groups, alongside IMG classifications. Unadjusted odds ratios (ORs) with 95% confidence intervals were calculated using White graduates and internal sub-ethnic baselines as comparators. Specialty-level ecological correlations (Spearmans rho) were performed to evaluate whether international workforce reliance moderated ethnic recruitment disparities. ResultsBetween 2021 and 2025, applicant volume expanded rapidly, with ethnic minority applicants and IMGs comprising numerical majorities. However, Asian and Black applicants experienced substantially lower odds of receiving training offers compared to White baseline applicants across multiple high-volume specialties (e.g., emergency medicine and anaesthetics at ST1, where Black applicants faced multi-fold reductions in success odds: OR 0.03 to 0.05, p<0.001). Granular analyses revealed notable intra-ethnic heterogeneity, including lower success among Pakistani and Bangladeshi applicants compared to Indian applicants. Furthermore, UK graduates maintained higher offer success than IMGs across most specialties. Ecological correlations demonstrated that higher international applicant reliance was moderately and significantly associated with wider recruitment disparities at higher training levels for Black applicants {rho}=-0.43, p=0.019). ConclusionsCentralised medical recruitment in England exhibits some persistent ethnic and international qualification disparities despite rising application diversity. The findings highlight the necessity of disaggregating ethnic groups and addressing subjective evaluation vulnerabilities within multi-stage recruitment processes to foster equity. Trial registrationNot applicable

papers.title: Can LLMs Succeed in National Dental Examinations? A Comprehensive Analysis of Performance, Strengths, and Limitations
papers.abstract: BackgroundLarge language models (LLMs) are increasingly explored as adjunct tools in graduate medical education, but their reliability for answering discipline-specific certification examinations remains incompletely characterized. In dentistry in China, the national dental examination serves as a milestone for stomatology trainees. Prior studies predominantly rely on single metric, limiting reproducibility and granularity. ObjectiveTo systematically evaluate the performance of five LLMs in answering the national standardized training examination for dental residents. MethodA total of 1,318 questions covering the six dentistry disciplines were selected. Five LLMs (DeepSeek-V3, DeepSeek-R1, Qwen3-32B, Claude 3.5, and GPT-4o) were evaluated via a single-response protocol on the Dify-based Chatflow framework. Performance combined human verification with automated scoring using the Retrieval-Augmented Generation Systems (RAGAS) framework across seven dimensions. Tasks involving question classification, key-point categorization, and instructional requirement summarization were designed to enable a horizontal comparison of models cognitive capabilities, assessed using inter-model consistency scores. ResultsDeepSeek-R1 achieved the highest correct choice rate (80.90%, p < 0.001) and answer correctness score (0.853, p < 0.001), significantly outperforming the others. All models exhibited limitations, including information insufficiency, redundancy, and hallucination-related issues (lowest 44.20% in DeepSeek-R1). In classification and summarization tasks, Claude 3.5 showed higher consistency scores (186/181) than Qwen3-32B (152/151). ConclusionEvaluated LLMs demonstrated good performance on dental examination questions and in executing tasks. DeepSeek-R1 consistently outperformed the others. While LLMs showed potential as supportive tools in dental education, further refinement and validation are needed before formal adoption in graduate medical educational and clinical training settings.

papers.title: A vulnerable space: Health professions education scholars' reflections on AI-use disclosure
papers.abstract: BackgroundAI use is growing by HPE scholars, and disclosure of that use is required by scientific ethics and journal policy. In spite of growing unease about the meaning, and meaningfulness, of AI-use disclosures in published manuscripts, little is known about how authors represent their AI use in published disclosure statements. Without such understanding, we are ill-equipped to redirect disclosure practices for increased sufficiency and sincerity, undermining efforts towards transparency in the era of AI-supported scholarship MethodsIn this descriptive qualitative study, 18 HPE researchers with experience disclosing generative AI use in publications from 2025-2026 were interviewed using Zoom. Data collection and thematic analysis proceeded iteratively, exploring participants experiences with AI use, their disclosure decisions, and evolving disclosure practices. ResultsParticipants reported a wide range of experience writing AI-use disclosures (from 1-16 disclosures/participant); in total 31 published disclosures were shared by participants and discussed during the interviews. Our analysis identified four themes: A spectrum of AI uses; Multi-factorial disclosure decisions; Discrepancies between actual and disclosed use; and Emotions around disclosure. These are described below and illustrated with representative excerpts from the dataset. DiscussionAI-disclosure practices take place at the intersection of shared ethical principles and situated pragmatic concerns. Disclosure is both an intellectual and an emotional practice, changing over time as AI use evolves and journal expectations develop. More generative uses may provoke divisive responses and are related to uncertainty about how to disclose, concern about disclosure penalties, and periodic use-disclosure discrepancies. Understanding how researchers are navigating these complexities may help our HPE community articulate clearer guidance for transparent and meaningful disclosure of AI-use in scholarly work. Reflective methodologies can help bring these issues to the surface of our fields ongoing conversations about AI use.

papers.title: Assessment of Clinical Competence Using AI-Standardized Clinical Examination
papers.abstract: BACKGROUNDAs artificial intelligence (AI) enters clinical practice, concerns about deskilling and never-skilling make the independent assessment of clinical competence increasingly important. The AI-Standardized Clinical Examination (ASCE) uses AI to simulate and score standardized clinical encounters, potentially overcoming some of the logistical and standardization constraints of conventional objective structured clinical examinations (OSCEs). Whether it provides valid and reliable assessment at scale is unknown. METHODSIn this prospective multicenter cohort study, final-year medical students from six French medical schools completed a 10-station ASCE six weeks before the national OSCE session. GPT-4o simulated standardized clinical partners; transcripts were subsequently scored by GPT-4.1 against faculty-defined rubrics. The primary outcome was the correlation between ASCE and national OSCE scores. Secondary outcomes were inter-rater reliability of expert transcript scoring, alignment of ASCE scores with expert ratings, and internal consistency. RESULTSAmong 948 enrolled students, 588 had paired ASCE and national OSCE scores. ASCE scores were correlated with national OSCE performance (Spearmans {rho}, 0.57; 95% CI, 0.51 to 0.63), with less than 1% of residual variance attributable to center (intraclass correlation coefficient, 0.01). Eight experts scored 20 randomly selected ASCE transcripts; Krippendorffs was 0.77 overall, 0.80 for clinical skills, and 0.70 for communication and attitude skills. Adding GPT-4.1 as an evaluator reduced by 0.02, and its scores did not differ significantly from those of individual experts. Internal consistency was 0.67 across 10 stations and was projected to approach 0.80 with 20 stations. CONCLUSIONSScores from an examination delivered and scored by AI were associated with performance on a national high-stakes OSCE, with minimal center-level variation, tentative agreement among expert raters, and automated scores that aligned with expert ratings. These results support AI delivery and scoring of clinical examinations, with expert review of automated scores. DescriptionIn what is, to our knowledge, the first prospective multicenter study to evaluate a clinical examination delivered and scored by AI against an independent national OSCE, 588 final-year medical students across six French medical schools completed an AI-Standardized Clinical Examination before the independent national OSCE. Scores correlated with national OSCE performance (Spearmans {rho}, 0.57), with negligible variation between centers, supporting AI-standardized assessment at scale.

papers.title: Prospective study on the organization and efficiency of online journal club
papers.abstract: BackgroundJournal clubs (JCs) are a popular education format. Interest in studying their impact is high, and authors often report positive results related to subjective parameters. Objective assessments of effectiveness are limited and contradictory. In this paper, we share our experience and describe our journal clubs effectiveness. MethodsWe conducted a prospective cohort study within our online journal club. Meetings followed a discussion-based format and were held via Zoom, with timing and topics determined by voting in the clubs Telegram chat. Enrolment occurred in waves and included an application, entry test, and interview. During each recruitment wave, both club members (treatment group) and applicants (control) completed an admission test assessing knowledge of evidence-based medicine and statistics. ResultsThe JC currently comprises 27 members. Over the past year, 76 meetings were held, with 75% of participants grading their experience with 9 or 10 on a ten-point scale. Multivariate analysis demonstrated non-significantly results (SMD = 0.19 (95% CI 0.004; 0.38), p = 0.046) among participants. However, in other adjusted models, differences between groups were not statistically significant (p > 0.05). ConclusionWhile the analysis of the subjective outcomes is consistent with findings from previous studies, the objective outcomes remain inconclusive. Further research is needed to refine the methodology for the organization and evaluation of journal clubs.

papers.title: Resident Physician Selection Practices and Professionalism-Related Difficulties in Japan: A Nationwide Cross-sectional Survey
papers.abstract: IntroductionPostgraduate clinical training is crucial for developing professional competence, communication skills, and effective teamwork. Although resident physician selection is crucial, little is known about how Japanese residency programs select residents and whether selection practices are associated with difficulties during training. MethodsWe conducted a nationwide cross-sectional survey of residency programs participating in Japans 2023 General Medicine In-Training Examination (GM-ITE). Program directors completed a questionnaire assessing selection methods, interview content, quality-assurance measures, and resident difficulties, defined as at least one postgraduate year 1 or 2 resident physician receiving disciplinary action or a severe warning. Free-text responses were coded using the Situation, Task, Action, and Result framework. Associations between selection methods and resident difficulties were examined using adjusted logistic regression models controlling for hospital type and number of GM-ITE examinees. ResultsOf 151 participating physician-selection programs, 150 provided valid responses. Interviews were used by 90.1% of programs and were identified as the most important selection component by 87.3%. Thirty-five programs (23.3%) reported difficulties with resident physicians, involving professionalism and workplace conduct including rule, ethics, or boundary violations, work avoidance or unavailability, and inappropriate communication. Use of applicants pre-clinical-clerkship computer-based test scores as a selection criterion was associated with resident difficulties (adjusted OR, 4.60; 95% CI, 1.50-14.11; P = 0.008; FDR-adjusted P = 0.048). No significant associations were observed for essays, academic tests, medical school grades, or personality assessment. Program-level GM-ITE total and domain scores did not differ significantly between programs with and without reported resident physician difficulties. DiscussionResident physician selection in Japan is highly interview-centered; reported difficulties were more often related to professionalism and workplace conduct than to knowledge deficits. Although these exploratory findings are program-level, they highlight the importance of strengthening the quality assurance processes in resident selection systems, particularly for assessing professionalism-related attributes in applicants. Practice PointsO_LIResident selection in Japan is strongly interview-centered; however, explicitly structured interviews, scoring systems, and rater calibration remain uncommon. C_LIO_LIProgram-reported resident difficulties primarily involved professionalism, communication, reliability, and workplace conduct rather than knowledge deficits. C_LIO_LIAcademic selection indicators alone may be insufficient to identify applicants who later require professionalism-related support. C_LIO_LIResidency programs should strengthen interview quality assurance through clearer structure, explicit evaluation criteria, and interviewer calibration. C_LIO_LISelection should be complemented by early identification, feedback, and longitudinal support during residency. C_LI

papers.title: Characterizing large language model generative artificial intelligence variability in the production of objective structured clinical examination stations
papers.abstract: BackgroundDesigning high-quality Objective Structured Clinical Examination (OSCE) stations is a time-consuming process. Generative artificial intelligence (AI) represents a promising path to accelerate content creation by automating the generation of scenarios. A growing number of AI tools is now available for this purpose. ObjectiveTo assess the variability between generative AI models in their ability to produce OSCE stations in the field of paediatrics. MethodsA structured prompt was developed based on the French national OSCE guidelines for medical education. Five distinct AI models were provided with this prompt, alongside the neonatal jaundice chapter from the French pediatric reference textbook, to generate 6 complete OSCE stations. Results. Prompt compliance was high for ChatGPT 5.1, ChatGPT 5.2, Gemini 3.0 Pro, and Claude Opus 4.5, while it was lower for Grok 4.1. Expert-rated quality was generally high, with few factual errors or missing information across models. However usability differed significantly between models. This was also true for several quality dimensions such as checklist clarity, embedding of checklist answers within vignettes, and ease of standardized patient formation. ChatGPT 5.1 required the most revisions and Gemini most often rated usable as is. Significant inter-model differences were observed in diagnostics, only with ChatGPT 5.1 sampling all three neonatal jaundice categories. Contextual variables showed systematic narrowing across models. Clinical grid density was consistent (10-12 items per station), but thematic distribution differed markedly. Soft skills coverage varied significantly across models (p=0.002), none of them consistently representing all communication competency domains. ConclusionLarge language models can generate structurally compliant OSCE stations, but surface compliance conceals substantive inter-model differences in diagnostic coverage, contextual diversity, and soft skills representation, that compromise content validity. No model currently meets the criteria for unsupervised deployment in a summative assessment bank. The choice of model carries pedagogical implications and expert curation remains essential before integration into high-stakes assessment workflows.

papers.title: Nudging Toward Precision Medical Education: Linking Diagnostic Exposures to Tailored Learning
papers.abstract: ProblemAuthentic patient encounters are the raw material of clinical learning, yet the educational resources learners receive are rarely keyed to the diagnoses in front of them, creating temporal and cognitive gaps. Precision medical education (PME) proposes delivering the right resource to the right learner at the right moment, but practical implementation in the clinical learning environment remains limited. ApproachWe developed DxMentor, an electronic health record (EHR)-integrated platform that captures each learners daily inpatient diagnostic exposures from documented International Classification of Diseases, Tenth Revision (ICD-10) codes. Artificial intelligence (AI) is used to match each diagnosis to an educator-curated formulary of micro-learning resources and board-style questions, and to PubMed-derived primary and synthesis literature converted into plain-language evidence summaries. A personalized email "nudge" is delivered before morning rounds, copying supervising attendings for residents, with engagement tracked longitudinally. We report implementation outcomes from July 2024-April 2026. OutcomesDxMentor evaluated 32,846 encounters from 335 medical students and 346 internal medicine residents, delivering 17,340 nudges containing 63,754 didactic resources, 17,038 question sets, and 23,594 summarized articles for approximately $390 in AI token costs. In a benchmarking sample, 91.5% (366/400) of diagnosis-resource pairs were rated relevant by physician-educators. Overall, 78.5% (12,393/15,793) of nudges were opened and 11.3% (1,955/17,340) had at least one click. Engagement was higher among residents than students (open: 80.7% vs. 65.8%; click-through: 12.7% vs. 3.1%; both P < .001), with substantial between-learner variability. Next StepsEmail opens and clicks are engagement proxies rather than measures of learning. We are therefore linking nudges to educational outcomes, testing alternative recommendation strategies and timing, and expanding to additional specialties and ambulatory and surgical settings. Teaser TextDxMentor integrates with the electronic health record to capture each learners daily diagnostic exposures, then uses AI to match diagnoses with tailored resources and evidence summaries--delivering automated email nudges before rounds to operationalize precision medical education at scale.

papers.title: Stakeholder perspectives on implementing a maternal health blended learning course for health care providers in Kenya, Nigeria and Tanzania
papers.abstract: BackgroundGood quality maternity care is critical in reducing maternal morbidity and mortality in regions with a high maternal and perinatal mortality. Building capacity of maternity care providers through in service training has been proven as effective in bridging the knowledge, competency, and skills gap during provision of maternity care. Meaningful involvement of stakeholder perspectives in the design and implementation of public health training programs heightens the prospects of achieving long term changes in practice and policy. MethodsTo explore stakeholder perspectives and experiences on the co-development of the antenatal-postnatal care course in Kenya, Nigeria, Tanzania. Data was collected through nine key informant interviews and observation notes between July - October 2022. Qualitative data was analysed in NVIVO software using inductive thematic analysis. ResultsStudy findings showed that stakeholders were receptive of the blended learning approach for training in antenatal and postnatal care describing it as accessible, and effective in improving knowledge and skills. Course facilitators and healthcare providers valued the interactive format, opportunities for pre-session preparation, and continuous support, which contributed to improved learning experiences and collaboration. ConclusionThis study highlighted the importance of involving stakeholders in the design and implementation of the antenatal-postnatal blended learning course in three countries. Eliciting feedback based on stakeholder experiences and incorporating it in real time strengthened the implementation of the blended learning course.

papers.title: Comparative evaluation of case studies and role-playing techniques in enhancing problem-based learning outcomes in Medical Biochemistry education- An educational randomized controlled trial
papers.abstract: Background and objectiveProblem-based learning (PBL) strategies such as case studies and role-playing are increasingly adopted in medical education to promote critical thinking, communication, and teamwork. However, comparative evidence regarding their effectiveness in medical biochemistry remains limited. This study aims to evaluate and compare the impact of case studies and role-playing on learning outcomes, engagement and skill development among first year MBBS students. Material and methodsAn educational randomized controlled trial (RCT) with a within-subjects crossover design was conducted in the Department of Biochemistry involving forty-five first-year MBBS students. Participants were randomly assigned to receive case studies and role-playing in a counterbalanced sequence. Learning outcomes were assessed using pre- and post-tests, a structured feedback questionnaire and qualitative reflections. Data were analysed using appropriate parametric and non-parametric tests, along with adjusted analysis using ANCOVA to account for baseline performance. ResultsAll participants completed both methods, with no significant difference in baseline knowledge between arms (P=0.12). Both case studies and role-playing produced significant pre- to post-test improvements (P<0.001). Unadjusted analyses showed higher learning gains with role-playing, but pre-crossover ANCOVA demonstrated comparable effectiveness after baseline adjustment. Exploratory pooled analysis suggested a moderate cumulative advantage for role-playing. Student feedback indicated higher engagement and perceived skill development with role-playing, while both methods were viewed as relevant and educationally valuable. ConclusionBoth case studies and role-playing were effective PBL strategies for improving understanding and application of medical biochemistry concepts. Although student feedback and unadjusted analyses indicated higher engagement with role-playing, adjusted analysis at initial exposure showed comparable effectiveness between the two methods. Role-playing supported interactive learning and AETCOM-related skills, while case studies strengthened structured analytical reasoning. A combined approach may therefore offer a balanced and comprehensive PBL framework in medical education.

papers.title: Building and Sustaining Scholarly Communities in Health Professions Education: Lessons from U.S. Academies
papers.abstract: IntroductionAcademic health centers have invested in academies and related structures to promote health professions education (HPE) scholarship, yet many struggle to sustain vibrant scholarly communities. We aimed to identify lessons for building and sustaining scholarly communities that support HPE scholarship. MethodsUsing a constructivist approach, we conducted a qualitative interview study in 2025 with leaders from across all four geographic regions of the U.S. Inclusion criteria required that participants direct an academy or other institutional structure intended to promote educational scholarship, and that they could speak to building and sustaining scholarly communities of practice in their local context. The Communities of Practice framework informed interview guide development and data interpretation. Interviews were audio-recorded, transcribed, de-identified, and analyzed using a six-phase thematic analysis process. ResultsTwenty-one academy leaders described five interrelated forms of leadership work that shaped sustainable scholarly communities: (1) building foundations that legitimize educational scholarship by securing institutional investment, leadership buy-in, succession planning, and guiding frameworks; (2) cultivating scholarly sanctuary to counter isolation through psychologically safe, inclusive communities; (3) making scholarship feasible under constraints by creating low-barrier entry points, translating value to leaders, and addressing time, productivity, and infrastructure barriers; (4) tending growth through layered, incremental development, including cohort programs, consultation, mentoring, grants, and flexible participation; and (5) making educational scholarship visible and valued through recognition, dissemination, and outcome tracking. DiscussionViewed through the Communities of Practice framework, the themes illuminate how leaders cultivated a shared domain of legitimate educational scholarship, a community of relational support, and a practice of tools, routines, and developmental infrastructure. The themes also reveal that sustainable communities of practice do not emerge from any single academy model, but from context-sensitive alignment of structure, culture, and incentives. Institutions seeking to strengthen HPE scholarship should invest in foundational resources, cultivate psychologically safe communities, adopt incremental growth strategies, and create pathways for recognition and dissemination that legitimize educational scholarship.

papers.title: Validation of an Assessment Scale for a Low-Tech Laparoscopic Appendectomy Simulation and Its Relevance for Formative Self-Assessment
papers.abstract: IntroductionLaparoscopic appendectomy is an ideal procedure for acquiring laparoscopic skills through simulation. Nevertheless, technical training is time consuming for surgical trainers to provide constructive feedback, but this could be improved by the development of validated tools that enable appropriate formative self-assessment. For this reason, we developed a structured assessment scale for a laparoscopic appendectomy exercise using a low-fidelity simulator. The objective of this study was to validate the scale for use in formative self-assessment. MethodsDuring laparoscopic simulation sessions in 2025-2026, participants with varying levels of experience performed a standardized laparoscopic appendectomy (LAP) exercise on a low-fidelity simulator. Performance was assessed through formative self- and external assessment using a specific scale derived from the OSATS (Objective Structured Assessment of Technical Skills) score. Content and construct validity, internal consistency, reproducibility, and reliability in both hetero- and self-assessment were analyzed. ResultsThirty-two participants were included in the validation study of the LAP scale, including 7 medical students, 17 residents in pediatric, visceral, urological, and gynecological surgery, and 8 practicing surgeons. The content of the scale was deemed relevant by 80% of the users. It demonstrated excellent construct validity, with scores increasing according to level of experience: 9.9 {+/-} 0.7 among students, 12.7 {+/-} 3.3 among junior residents, 16.6 {+/-} 3.3 among experienced residents, and 18.8 {+/-} 0.9 among practicing surgeons (p < 0.0001). Reproducibility and internal consistency were significant, while inter- and intra-rater reliability were excellent (correlation coefficients r = 0.90 and 0.91; p < 0.0001), as was the correlation between external and self-assessment (r = 0.81; p < 0.0001). Self-assessment was more reliable among experienced learners than among novices. ConclusionThis standardized LAP scale is validated for both external and self-assessment, the latter requiring prior training to be reliable and formative.
